article.title: Why Simpson’s Paradox Can Reverse the Story in Aggregated Data
article.why: 理解 aggregate metric、mix shift 與 within-segment performance。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Simpson’s paradox describes a situation in which an overall trend changes or reverses after data is divided into meaningful groups. It is not just a statistical curiosity. It appears whenever an aggregate metric combines populations with different baseline levels and changing weights.

Imagine a retailer comparing conversion rates between two years. Overall conversion rises from 4.8 percent to 5.1 percent, so the first conclusion is that performance improved. Now separate new customers from returning customers. Within new customers, conversion fell. Within returning customers, conversion also fell. How can the total still increase?

The answer is composition. Returning customers usually convert at a much higher rate. If the second year contains a much larger share of returning customers, the overall average can rise even though both groups perform worse. The aggregate metric is a weighted average, and the weights changed.

The reverse pattern is also possible. Every major segment can improve while the total declines if traffic shifts toward a segment with a lower baseline conversion rate. This often happens during expansion. A marketing campaign may bring many first-time visitors who convert less frequently than loyal customers. The business can improve within both segments while the overall rate falls.

This matters because management actions depend on the diagnosis. If total conversion falls because every segment got worse, teams should investigate product experience, price, or operations. If each segment improved but the mix shifted toward harder-to-convert users, the decline may reflect successful top-of-funnel growth rather than a broken product.

The same logic applies to average spend, churn, approval rates, defect rates, hospital outcomes, and employee performance. Any aggregate number can move because of two forces: changes within groups and changes in the proportion of each group.

A practical workflow starts with the total metric, then identifies segments with different baseline levels. Common candidates include customer tenure, age, geography, channel, device, store type, risk class, and time period. Compare the metric within those groups and track how their weights changed.

However, analysts should not split data endlessly until they find a preferred story. Excessive slicing creates small samples and unstable patterns. Segments should be chosen because they are meaningful to the data-generating process, not because they produce an interesting result.

Regression can help estimate conditional relationships, but it does not remove the need to understand composition. Control variables should be selected carefully. A variable that is caused by the treatment or lies on the causal pathway may create a different bias if controlled mechanically.

One useful decomposition is to ask how much of the total change comes from within-segment performance and how much comes from mix shift. Even a simple reweighting exercise can answer this. Keep segment weights fixed at the previous year and apply current-year segment rates. Then compare that standardized result with the observed total.

This approach is particularly helpful in year-over-year customer analysis. If the age distribution, channel share, region mix, or rank composition changed, comparing only total averages can confuse population change with behavioral change.

The core lesson is that an aggregate number is not a pure property of individual behavior. It is a combination of behavior and population structure. Before saying “customers improved” or “the campaign failed,” ask whether the people being averaged are distributed the same way.

Simpson’s paradox is therefore a reminder to inspect the denominator, the groups, and their weights. A total can be mathematically correct and still support the wrong business story if composition is ignored.
